title: SK2Decompile: Two-Phase Binary Decoding
one_liner: Decode compiled programs back to readable source by first recovering structure, then filling in names that match the original semantics.
lead: When you compile a program, the binary loses all the original variable and function names—they become anonymous numbers. SK2Decompile solves this by breaking the decoding task into two independent steps: first, recover the skeleton (control flow, data structures), then add the skin (names that match the original code's intent). Each step uses a language model trained with reinforcement learning to produce code that a real compiler accepts and semantically matches the original.

paras: When a program is compiled, the names of variables, functions, and types vanish—the binary only contains memory addresses and operations. A naive approach tries to decode binary directly to source code in one shot, but it fails because the model has to guess the structure and names simultaneously. It cannot tell what matters (control flow, data types) from what is noise (naming choices), so it produces code that is either syntactically broken or semantically incoherent.

The real problem: asking a model to solve two hard problems at once (restore structure; invent names) means it cannot specialize at either, and small errors in one cascade into large errors in the other.

callout.html: Split the decoding task into two phases: first recover the program structure cleanly, then name variables to match the original semantics.

steps.text: Convert source code to an abstract syntax tree, then replace all variable/function names with generic placeholders, preserving structure.
Teach a language model to translate binary to this obfuscated skeleton, using reinforcement learning that rewards compilable output.
Feed binary to the Structure Recovery model, producing intermediate code with correct control flow but no real names.
Teach a second language model to replace placeholders with real names, rewarded for semantic similarity to originals.
Apply Identifier Naming to the skeleton, resulting in decoded source that runs and reads like the original.

paras: Instead of asking one model to decode everything at once, SK2Decompile splits the problem into two sequential steps, each with its own model and its own reinforcement learning objective. The object being changed is the architecture of the decompilation pipeline itself—from monolithic to two-phase.

hidden.name: Structural coherence (compilability + type correctness)
paras: The paper measures a hidden quantity that traditional decoding ignores: how much the recovered code matches the original program's structure. This is not about names; it is about whether loops, branches, function calls, and data types are in the right place.

The paper estimates this by running the recovered code through a real compiler. If the compiler accepts it and type-checking passes, the structure is coherent. Reinforcement learning then rewards the model for producing output that passes these checks.

heat.caption: Darker means more important to structural coherence. Highlighted cells are what the compiler actually checks.

reads.html: A program's skeleton is the control flow (which code runs when) and data structures (arrays, records, types). Two programs with the same structure but different variable names are the same program. Structural coherence means the skeleton is correct and will compile.

The paper uses compiler feedback as the signal for structural coherence. Specifically, the compiler can check whether the generated intermediate representation is syntactically valid and type-safe. This is what drives the reinforcement learning reward in Phase 1.

mechanism.h2: Why separating structure from naming works
paras: The mechanism works because structure and naming are two orthogonal problems. When a model tries to solve both at once, it spreads its learning capacity thin—every error in structure production corrupts the names, because the model cannot tell whether a poor name resulted from structural confusion or poor naming, and every naming error makes it harder to verify that the structure is correct, since a misnamed variable may hide a control-flow bug.

By decoupling them, each model can specialize. The Structure Recovery model focuses only on translating binary opcodes to high-level control flow and data types, ignoring the naming problem entirely by using placeholders. This is a simpler signal: the compiler tells you immediately if the structure is wrong. The Identifier Naming model then operates on a clean, validated skeleton, so it only has to match semantics of names to the original code, without worrying whether the underlying structure is correct.

Reinforcement learning in each phase explicitly rewards correctness of that phase's goal. In Phase 1, the reward is compilability: does the compiler accept this output without errors? In Phase 2, the reward is semantic similarity: how close are the predicted names to the original variable names? Separating these rewards means each model learns a sharper objective.

math.words: Total loss = cross-entropy loss (standard language modeling) + reinforcement learning reward based on compiler feedback (Phase 1) or name similarity (Phase 2)
math.equation: L_total = L_CE(theta) + beta * R(output) where R(output) is either compiler_accepts(output) or semantic_similarity(predicted_names, original_names)
symbols: standard cross-entropy loss, measures how often the model predicts the next token correctly
how much weight to give the reinforcement learning reward
reward signal: in Phase 1, a score from the compiler; in Phase 2, how similar the names are
the weights of the language model

worked.title: A tiny worked example (Phase 1 Structure Recovery)
lines: Binary input: a sequence of 20 opcodes for integer addition, memory read, loop branch.
Model predicts next token (IR snippet) at each step.
Cross-entropy loss penalizes wrong predictions: model says 'int x' but should say 'int index', penalty = 0.8.
Compiler runs on full predicted skeleton: accepts it, no type errors. Reward = +1.0.
Total loss for this batch = sum of cross-entropy penalties (0.8 + 0.6 + ... ≈ 5.2) + beta * 1.0. If beta=0.5, total = 5.2 + 0.5 = 5.7.
Model learns to balance: predict tokens accurately AND produce compilable output.

math.note: Separating the two phases means each can use a specialized reward: Phase 1 measures if the structure compiles, Phase 2 measures if the names are semantically right.

charts.title: Naive one-shot decoding
charts.note: Trying to solve both problems simultaneously means the model spreads its effort and fails at both. Structure errors contaminate name prediction.

charts.title: Two-phase (SK2Decompile)
charts.note: Decoupling structure recovery from naming allows each phase to specialize, because each model can focus entirely on its own goal and its own training signal without confusion. Compiler feedback ensures Phase 1 correctness before Phase 2 even starts, so Phase 2 only has to match names, not fix broken logic.

items.html: If the Structure Recovery model generates IR that the compiler rejects (e.g., mismatched parentheses, type errors), the reinforcement learning signal fails to guide improvement. Mitigation: use a very strict compiler reward and pre-train heavily on valid code.

Even if the skeleton is structurally perfect, the Identifier Naming model may replace placeholders with names that do not match the original semantics (e.g., calling a counter variable 'output_file'). This happens if the RL reward is too weak. Mitigation: ensure the similarity check between predicted and original names (measured by comparing how close the meanings are) strongly penalizes off-target names.

The skeleton phase uses generic placeholders (func_1, var_2). If those placeholders erase all hints about what variables are used for, Phase 2 cannot learn how to name them. For example, erasing a comment or annotation that says 'accumulator' means the naming model has to guess the purpose from context alone. The trade-off is worth it (generic names force the structure to stand on its own), but it is still a limitation.

Train Phase 1 until the compiler consistently accepts the output, then train Phase 2 on that high-quality skeleton. Use separate, well-tuned RL rewards for each phase. Test both phases on a held-out set of binaries not seen during training.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small decompiler that takes a simple C program, compiles it to binary, then runs SK2Decompile's two phases to recover source. Measure whether the recovered code compiles and whether variable names match the originals.
demo.metric_eq: re-executability = (recovered_code compiles and runs correctly) / (total_test_cases); name_accuracy = (predicted_name == original_name) / (total_identifiers)
demo.closing: The key moment is seeing that Phase 1 produces valid but named-generically code, and Phase 2 transforms it into human-readable source with the original semantics. This proves the value of decoupling.
